1ch.background: 1 Chronicles, traditionally attributed to Ezra, was composed after the return from exile to remind the returned people of their identity and heritage. The first nine chapters are genealogies, tracing the lineages of Israel's tribes from Adam down to the return from exile. The remainder (chapters 10-29) passes over most of Saul's reign and focuses on the history of David as king, especially his preparations for building the temple - gathering materials, organizing the priestly and Levitical divisions, establishing the ministry of the singers - and his handing over of the kingdom to Solomon.
1ch.keyPoints: Through the genealogies and David's devotion to building the temple, the book grounds the people's faith and sense of identity in the worship of the temple, the priestly order, and the everlasting covenant with the house of David.

1co.background: 1 Corinthians was written by Paul during his ministry in Ephesus, after he learned of the many troubles disturbing the church in Corinth, and it addresses those problems one by one. The letter is arranged by topic: it rebukes the divisions and factions in the church (chapters 1-4); addresses sexual immorality, lawsuits among believers, and matters of marriage (chapters 5-7); teaches that eating food offered to idols must take account of weaker brothers (chapters 8-10); instructs on order in worship, the Lord's Supper, and the use of spiritual gifts, holding up love as the governing principle for exercising them (chapters 11-14); and in its final section sets forth the resurrection of Christ and the hope of believers' future resurrection (chapter 15), closing with instructions about the collection (chapter 16).
1co.keyPoints: The letter shows that the church's unity is found in Christ and that spiritual gifts must be exercised in love; it also establishes Christ's resurrection as the foundation of the faith, giving believers the hope of their own resurrection.

1jo.background: 1 John was written by the apostle John in his later years, addressing a heresy that denied Christ had truly come in the flesh. The letter offers a series of tests for distinguishing genuine faith: walking in the light, loving one another, keeping God's commandments, and rejecting the world's sinful desires. Through these, John strengthens believers' assurance of eternal life and urges them to discern the spirit of true and false prophets. He emphasizes that God is love, and that because believers love God they must also love one another - this alone demonstrates a life truly in fellowship with him.
1jo.keyPoints: The central theme is a set of tests for genuine faith - walking in the light, keeping God's commandments, and loving one another - given so that believers may know with certainty that they have eternal life.

1ki.background: 1 Kings records the history from Solomon's accession to the throne through the division of the kingdom and on to roughly the mid-ninth century BC; Jewish tradition holds that Jeremiah compiled the book from earlier records. The first section (chapters 1-11) tells of Solomon succeeding to the throne, asking for wisdom, building the temple, and presiding over a kingdom at the height of its power - yet in his old age his foreign wives lead him into idolatry, sowing the seeds of the coming division. The second section (chapters 12-22) tells how Rehoboam and Jeroboam bring about the split into the northern and southern kingdoms, interweaves the histories of the kings of both, and dwells at length on the prophet Elijah's confrontation with the prophets of Baal under the reign of Ahab and Jezebel.
1ki.keyPoints: The central theme is that the nation's rise and fall hinges on the faithfulness of king and people to God; the book warns against the sin of idolatry and shows God upholding his covenant faithfulness through the prophets.

1pe.background: 1 Peter was written by the apostle Peter to believers scattered across several provinces of Asia Minor who were suffering for their faith. The letter encourages believers to hold on to a living hope amid persecution and trials, following the example of Christ's own suffering. Because they have been chosen and made a royal priesthood and a holy nation, they are called to holiness in word and deed, and to humble submission and mutual love in their relationships as husbands and wives, servants, and citizens. It closes with an exhortation to elders to shepherd the flock and to stay alert against the enemy.
1pe.keyPoints: The central theme is living hope: through Christ's resurrection believers receive a living, eternal hope, and are called to endure suffering patiently after Christ's example and to live a holy, blessed life.

1sa.background: 1 Samuel records the history from the close of the era of the judges through the reign of Saul; tradition attributes parts of it to Samuel, Nathan, and Gad (compare 1 Chronicles 29:29). The first section (chapters 1-7) tells of Samuel's birth, the corruption of Eli's priestly household, and the ark's capture and return. The middle section (chapters 8-15) recounts the people's demand for a king, Saul's anointing, and his rejection by God for disobedience. The final section (chapters 16-31) tells of David's anointing, his slaying of Goliath, and Saul's jealous pursuit of him, closing with Saul's defeat and suicide in battle.
1sa.keyPoints: The central theme is that God looks on the heart, not the outward appearance, and that obedience is better than sacrifice; Saul is rejected for his disobedience, preparing the way for David to receive the kingdom.

1th.background: 1 Thessalonians was written by Paul from Corinth during his second missionary journey - possibly his earliest letter - addressed to the persecuted church at Thessalonica, prompted by Timothy's report on their condition. The first section (chapters 1-3) recalls the founding of the church, commends the believers' faith, hope, and love, and gives thanks for the good news Timothy brought back; the second section (chapters 4-5) exhorts them to holy living, mutual love, and diligent work, and teaches the hope of the Lord's return - that those who have died will rise first, and those who are alive will be caught up together with the Lord - urging believers to stay watchful as they wait.
1th.keyPoints: The central message is the hope of the Lord's certain return: it comforts believers facing persecution and the grief of losing loved ones, and urges them to live watchful, holy, and diligent lives as they wait for Christ.

1ti.background: 1 Timothy is a pastoral letter Paul wrote to Timothy, the young pastor of the church at Ephesus, to guide him in establishing order in the church and standing against false teaching. The letter covers: a warning against false teachers and legalism (chapter 1); instruction on public prayer and the roles of men and women in the church (chapter 2); the qualifications for overseers (elders) and deacons (chapter 3); Timothy's call to be an example to believers and devote himself to reading and teaching Scripture (chapter 4); principles for how the church should treat widows, elders, and servants (chapters 5-6), along with a warning against the love of money and an exhortation to hold fast to sound doctrine and fight the good fight.
1ti.keyPoints: The central message is establishing sound order in the church and holding fast to right doctrine, standing against false teaching and the love of money through a life of godliness.

2ch.background: 2 Chronicles continues 1 Chronicles, sharing its focus on the temple and worship, and was likewise composed after the return from exile. The opening section (chapters 1-9) records Solomon's building and dedication of the temple, together with his wisdom and splendor. The rest (chapters 10-36) traces the history of the kings of Judah, passing over the northern kingdom of Israel, and centers on each king's attitude toward the temple's worship and the law - those who honored the temple and kept the law were blessed, while those who rebelled and turned to idols brought disaster - down to the destruction of Jerusalem and the exile of the people. The book closes with the decree of Cyrus, king of Persia, permitting the return and the rebuilding of the temple, ending on a note of hope.
2ch.keyPoints: The message running throughout the book is that honoring the temple's worship and humbly repenting bring God's favor, while forsaking the law for idolatry brings judgment.

2co.background: 2 Corinthians is Paul's most personal and emotionally candid letter to the church in Corinth, written after he left Ephesus and was waiting in Macedonia for Titus to bring back news of the church. Paul begins by describing the comfort God gives in affliction, and explains his heart concerning his earlier severe letter and his delayed visit (chapters 1-7); he then urges the Corinthians to give generously toward the collection for the saints in Jerusalem (chapters 8-9); and in the final section he defends his apostolic authority against false apostles, recounting the sufferings and visions he has endured, and testifying that "when I am weak, then I am strong" (chapters 10-13).
2co.keyPoints: The central message is that God gives comfort in suffering, and his power is made perfect in human weakness; Paul points to this truth as evidence of genuine apostolic authority and self-giving service.

2jo.background: 2 John is a very brief letter from the apostle John, addressed to "the elect lady," who may represent an individual believer or a local church. John urges her to walk in the truth and to love one another, while issuing a firm warning not to welcome or even greet false teachers who deny that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, lest she share in their wicked deeds. He closes with the hope of visiting in person to talk face to face.
2jo.keyPoints: The central theme is holding truth and love together, with a firm warning against welcoming false teachers who deny that Christ came in the flesh, lest one share in their evil deeds.

2ki.background: 2 Kings continues 1 Kings - Jewish tradition likewise attributes its compilation to Jeremiah - and records the history of the divided kingdom down to its downfall. The first section (chapters 1-17) tells of Elisha succeeding to Elijah's prophetic ministry and interweaves the histories of the northern and southern kings, closing with the fall of the northern kingdom of Israel to Assyria in 722 BC because of its idolatry (chapter 17). The second section (chapters 18-25) follows the kings of Judah alone; though Hezekiah and Josiah carry out religious reforms, the kingdom's persistent rebellion finally brings it down to Babylon in 586 BC, the temple is destroyed, and the people are carried into exile. The closing chapter briefly notes the release of Jehoiachin, leaving a thread of hope.
2ki.keyPoints: The central theme is that persistent rebellion brings God's judgment, national ruin, and exile - yet God still preserves the line of David, preserving hope.

2pe.background: 2 Peter is the apostle Peter's farewell letter, written as he faced death, urging believers to grow in true knowledge and to live out godly virtue. It issues a strong warning against false teachers who have infiltrated the church, greedy and immoral, who will face judgment and destruction. The final chapter addresses scoffers who will arise in the last days questioning the promise of Christ's return; Peter affirms that the day of the Lord will surely come, and urges believers to watch and wait, growing in grace and in the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.
2pe.keyPoints: The central theme is a warning against false teachers and firm confidence that the Lord will return: believers are urged to grow in truth and virtue, watching and waiting for the day of the Lord.

2sa.background: 2 Samuel continues 1 Samuel, recounting the history of David's reign after Saul's death — first as king over Judah, then anointed king over all Israel — spanning roughly forty years on the throne. The first part (chapters 1-10) tells of his rise: he captures Jerusalem as his capital, and the LORD makes an everlasting covenant of kingship with him. The second part (chapters 11-20) turns to his fall: his sin with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah bring a chain of family tragedy - Amnon's rape of Tamar, Absalom's rebellion, and David's forced flight from Jerusalem. A closing appendix (chapters 21-24) records a famine, a roster of David's mighty men, and the plague brought on by his census.
2sa.keyPoints: The heart of the book is the LORD's everlasting covenant with David, the foundation of the messianic promise; it also shows sin's heavy cost, and God's faithful, disciplining rule even amid human weakness.

2th.background: 2 Thessalonians was written by Paul a short time later to the same church, whose members had become alarmed by the mistaken belief that the day of the Lord had already come, and some had even stopped working and were living in idleness. The first chapter commends their endurance and faith under persecution and declares that God will surely vindicate the righteous; the second chapter corrects their misunderstanding, clarifying that a great rebellion and the revealing of the "man of lawlessness" (who exalts himself as God) must come before the Lord's return; and the final chapter urges believers to stand firm and watchful, while sternly rebuking those living in idleness, calling them to work quietly and earn their own living.
2th.keyPoints: The central message is to clarify the order of events surrounding the Lord's return and correct end-times panic, urging believers to hold fast to sound teaching, remain watchful and steadfast, and live diligently.

2ti.background: 2 Timothy is Paul's final letter, written from a Roman prison as he awaited martyrdom, and its earnest tone is filled with parting instructions. Paul urges Timothy: not to be ashamed of Paul's sufferings, but to guard the truth entrusted to him by the power of the Holy Spirit (chapter 1); to be a good soldier of Christ Jesus, faithfully preaching the word and rightly handling the truth (chapter 2); to guard against the corruption of the last days and hold fast to the Scriptures he has known from childhood (chapter 3); and in the final chapter Paul looks back on his life, declaring that he has "fought the good fight, finished the race, and kept the faith," urging Timothy to come to him quickly.
2ti.keyPoints: The central message is faithful endurance in guarding and proclaiming the truth, even unto death; believers are urged to follow Paul's example in fighting the good fight and finishing the race.

3jo.background: 3 John is a personal letter from the apostle John to Gaius, commending him for his loving hospitality toward traveling gospel workers and his support for the work of the truth. John also rebukes Diotrephes, a man in the church who loves to be first, refuses to welcome the traveling teachers, and slanders the apostle himself; by contrast he commends Demetrius, who is well spoken of and eager to help. The letter closes with John's hope of seeing Gaius soon to speak with him face to face.
3jo.keyPoints: The central theme is commendation of loving hospitality toward those who serve the truth, together with a warning against the proud spirit of one who loves to be first and refuses to welcome fellow believers.

act.background: Acts is Luke's second volume, continuing directly from the Gospel of Luke, and records the founding of the church after the coming of the Holy Spirit and the spread of the gospel from Jerusalem to Rome. The book falls into two main parts: the first (chapters 1-12) centers on Peter, recounting the rise of the Jerusalem church and its expansion through the Spirit's power amid persecution; the second (chapters 13-28) centers on Paul, recording his three missionary journeys, the turning of the Gentiles to Christ, and his eventual imprisonment and ministry in Rome. Throughout, the book makes clear that the Holy Spirit is the driving power behind the church's mission.
act.keyPoints: The central message is that the Holy Spirit empowers the gospel to break beyond Jewish boundaries and spread to every nation; the church continues to grow in strength even amid persecution.

amo.background: Amos, the author, was a shepherd from Tekoa in Judah who was called to preach to the northern kingdom of Israel during the reign of Jeroboam II, a time when the nation was prosperous but morally corrupt. The book opens by pronouncing judgment on Damascus and other surrounding nations, and finally on Israel itself (chapters 1-2); it then rebukes Israel's social injustice and hollow worship (chapters 3-6); five visions follow, warning that judgment is coming (chapter 7 through the first part of chapter 9); and the book closes with the promise that the house of David will be restored and God's people brought back to their land (latter part of chapter 9).
amo.keyPoints: The book sharply condemns social injustice and empty religious ritual, calling instead for 'judgment to run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream' - genuine justice matters more than sacrifice.

col.background: Colossians was written by Paul while in prison, addressed to the church at Colossae — a church Paul had not personally founded, but which was planted through the preaching of Epaphras. At the time, the church was being influenced by a false teaching that mixed in angel worship, legalistic regulations, and human philosophy, diminishing Christ's rightful place. The letter falls into two parts: the doctrinal section (chapters 1–2) emphasizes that Christ is the full expression of God himself, head over all creation and head of the church, and that believers are already made complete in him; the practical section (chapters 3–4) exhorts believers to put off the old self and put on the new, addressing household relationships between husbands and wives, parents and children, and masters and servants, before closing with greetings and instructions to exchange letters with the church at Laodicea.
col.keyPoints: The core message is the supreme sufficiency of Christ: he is the full expression of God and head over all things; believers are already complete in him, and are called to reject false, man-made regulations and live out a new life united with him.

dan.background: Daniel tells of Daniel's exile to Babylon as a young man, and his service under Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar, and other kings, through into the Persian period. The book falls into two parts: chapters 1-6 are narrative, telling how Daniel and his three friends remained faithful to God and refused to worship idols, including the miracle of Daniel's deliverance from the lions' den; chapters 7-12 consist of visions - the four beasts, the seventy weeks, and more - revealing the rise and fall of future kingdoms and the ultimate triumph of God's kingdom.
dan.keyPoints: The book displays God's sovereign rule over history and the rise and fall of nations, encouraging believers to remain faithful to the end even in a pagan environment.

deu.background: Deuteronomy, traditionally attributed to Moses, comprises his farewell addresses on the plains of Moab, given just before Israel entered Canaan, in which he renews the Sinai covenant with the new generation. The book falls into four parts: a review of the wilderness history (chapters 1-4); a restatement of the Ten Commandments and the details of the law (chapters 5-26); a proclamation of blessing for obedience and cursing for rebellion, together with the renewal of the covenant at Moab (chapters 27-30); and the closing section, recounting Moses' commissioning of Joshua, his song and blessing over the twelve tribes, and his death on Mount Nebo (chapters 31-34).
deu.keyPoints: The heart of the book is the renewal of the covenant and the call to love God alone - "Hear, O Israel" - stressing that obedience brings blessing and rebellion brings a curse.

ecc.background: Ecclesiastes is traditionally attributed to Solomon in his later years, its author styling himself "the Preacher" as he reflects, from the vantage point of a wise king, on the meaning of life. The book surveys pleasure, wealth, wisdom, and toil, and finds them all "vanity" under the sun, since all alike end in death; only the fear of God and the keeping of his commandments constitute the whole duty of man. Opening with the words "vanity of vanities" and closing with a call to remember the Creator, the book's seemingly bleak exploration ultimately leads to faith resting in the eternal God.
ecc.keyPoints: The core message is that apart from God, all worldly toil and pleasure end in vanity; the whole duty of man is to fear God and keep his commandments.

eph.background: Ephesians was written by Paul while imprisoned in Rome, addressed to the church at Ephesus (possibly as a circular letter meant to be read among a number of churches), and it unfolds the mystery and exalted status of the church as the body of Christ. The doctrinal section (chapters 1-3) describes how God chose and redeemed believers in Christ, uniting Jew and Gentile together in him as members of the same household of God; the practical section (chapters 4-6) urges believers toward unity of mind, putting off the old self and putting on the new, addresses the duties of husbands and wives, parents and children, and masters and servants, and closes with the call to put on the whole armor of God to stand against the devil's schemes.
eph.keyPoints: The central message is that the church is the body of Christ, in whom Jew and Gentile are made one; believers are called to live out that calling and to stand firm in spiritual battle clothed in the armor of God.

est.background: Esther, whose author is unknown, tells how the Jews scattered throughout Persia and not among those who had returned to the land were preserved from annihilation during the reign of King Ahasuerus. The first part (chapters 1-2) recounts the deposing of Queen Vashti and the rise of the Jewish girl Esther to become queen in her place. The next section (chapters 3-5) tells how Haman, enraged that Mordecai would not bow to him, plotted to destroy the Jews, and how Mordecai urged Esther to risk her life and plead their case before the king. The final section (chapters 6-10) recounts the unraveling of Haman's plot and his downfall, the deliverance of the Jews, and the establishment of the Feast of Purim to commemorate it. God's name never appears in the book, yet his hidden providence is evident on every page.
est.keyPoints: Though God's name is never mentioned, his wondrous providence works behind the scenes to faithfully preserve his people - encouraging us to act in faith even amid hardship.

exo.background: Exodus, traditionally attributed to Moses, records how, after four hundred years of slavery in Egypt, God delivered the Israelites and led them out toward Mount Sinai. The book falls into three parts: the first (chapters 1-18) tells how God, through Moses, sent the ten plagues and instituted the Passover, then led the people through the Red Sea and the wilderness toward Sinai; the second (chapters 19-24) records God making a covenant with Israel at Sinai and giving the Ten Commandments and the law; the third (chapters 25-40) gives instructions for building the tabernacle, interrupted by the people's covenant-breaking sin of worshiping the golden calf, and closes with the glory of the LORD filling the tabernacle to dwell among his people.
exo.keyPoints: The central theme is God's deliverance of his covenant people and his giving of the law; through the tabernacle he comes to dwell among them, displaying both his redemption and his presence.

eze.background: Ezekiel, a priest-prophet exiled to Babylon, was called by the Kebar River after his deportation in 597 BC, and delivered his message to the Judean exiles. The book falls into three parts: chapters 1-24 announce that Jerusalem will fall on account of its sin; chapters 25-32 pronounce judgment on the surrounding nations; and chapters 33-48 turn to promises of restoration, including the vision of the valley of dry bones coming to life, the regathering of Israel, and, at the close, a detailed vision of the rebuilt temple and the return of God's glory.
eze.keyPoints: The book emphasizes God's holiness and glory, and that each person bears responsibility for their own sin; it promises a new heart and a new spirit, and that in the end God will dwell among his people once more.

ezr.background: Ezra is traditionally attributed to Ezra the scribe, and records the history of the Jewish return from exile during the Persian era. The first part (chapters 1-6) tells how King Cyrus issued a decree permitting the return, and how Zerubbabel and Joshua led the first group of exiles back to Jerusalem; despite opposition from their enemies, the temple was completed in the reign of King Darius. The second part (chapters 7-10) tells of Ezra himself, who led a second group back under King Artaxerxes and taught the people the law. When he found that the people had intermarried with foreigners and adopted their customs, he led them to confess their sin, repent, and put away their foreign wives, setting themselves apart as holy once more.
ezr.keyPoints: God faithfully fulfilled his promise by bringing his people back to rebuild the temple; Ezra devoted himself to studying, obeying, and teaching the law, leading the people to set themselves apart as holy.

gal.background: Galatians was written by Paul to the churches of Galatia after Judaizing teachers began insisting that Gentile believers had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses in order to be saved, corrupting the truth of the gospel. Paul first recounts his own call to preach the gospel, showing that the gospel he preaches came directly through revelation from Christ (chapters 1-2); he then draws on Old Testament examples to show that justification comes by faith and not by works of the law, the law itself having served as a guardian to lead people to Christ (chapters 3-4); and in the closing section he urges believers to walk by the Spirit - free from the law's bondage, yet not to indulge the flesh - and lists the fruit of the Spirit (chapters 5-6).
gal.keyPoints: The central message is justification by faith, not by works of the law; having been set free by Christ, believers are called to walk by the Spirit and bear the fruit of the Spirit.

gen.background: Genesis, traditionally attributed to Moses, records the history from the creation of heaven and earth to Israel's sojourn in Egypt, and is the first book of the Pentateuch. It falls into two parts: the primeval history (chapters 1-11) tells of creation, humanity's fall, the judgment of the flood, and the tower of Babel, tracing how sin entered the world; the patriarchal narratives (chapters 12-50) recount the calling and covenant story of four generations - Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph - through whom God promises to bless all nations. The book closes with Jacob's whole family moving to Egypt because of famine, setting the stage for Exodus.
gen.keyPoints: The heart of the book is God's creation and his covenant promise: he chooses Abraham's descendants as the channel of blessing for all nations, showing that even amid human sin and failure, he remains faithfully sovereign.

hab.background: Little is known of Habakkuk, the author, and the book was written near the end of the seventh century BC, as Babylon was rising to power. The book centers on a dialogue between the prophet and God: in chapter 1, Habakkuk is troubled and questions God over the injustice rampant in Judah, and God reveals that he will raise up Babylon to bring judgment; in chapter 2, Habakkuk asks further why God would use a nation more wicked than Judah to punish it, and God promises that the wicked will ultimately fall while the righteous will live by faith; the final chapter is a psalm-like prayer of Habakkuk's, expressing joyful trust in God even amid harsh circumstances, because he has come to know him.
hab.keyPoints: At the heart of the book is 'the just shall live by his faith' - even when God's ways are not understood and circumstances are hard, believers are to trust him in faith and find their joy in him.

hag.background: Haggai, the author, was the first prophet after the return from exile, and he prophesied to Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, and Joshua the high priest, in the second year of Darius, king of Persia (520 BC). Although the people had returned sixteen years earlier, they excused themselves by saying the time had not yet come, busying themselves with their own houses while the temple lay in ruins. The first chapter rebukes the people for their misplaced priorities, which had brought on crop failure and hardship, and the people promptly resumed the work; the second chapter records God's promise that the latter glory of the temple would surpass the former, along with the promise to bless and cleanse the people and to establish Zerubbabel as a signet ring.
hag.keyPoints: At the heart of the book is putting God's house first: once the people obeyed and resumed building the temple, God promised his presence, his blessing, and greater glory to come.

heb.background: The authorship of Hebrews has never been settled by tradition. It was written to Hebrew believers facing persecution who were tempted to abandon their faith and return to Judaism. The letter argues at length that Christ is superior to the angels, to Moses, and to the Levitical priesthood - he is God's final and complete revelation, and as great high priest he offered a single sacrifice that accomplished eternal redemption. Interwoven with this argument are several severe warnings urging readers to hold fast in faith and not fall away; chapter 11 catalogs the heroes of faith from the Old Testament as examples, and the letter closes by urging a life of gratitude, holiness, and mutual care lived out in faith.
heb.keyPoints: The central truth is that Christ is supreme over all things and is the perfect high priest, whose single sacrifice accomplished redemption once for all; believers are urged to persevere in faith to the end rather than drift away.

hos.background: Hosea, the author, was a prophet in the northern kingdom of Israel during its final years, active from the reign of Jeroboam II until shortly before the kingdom's fall. God commanded him to marry Gomer, a promiscuous woman, and through the breakdown and eventual restoration of that marriage he portrayed Israel's unfaithfulness to the LORD in turning after idols (chapters 1-3). The rest of the book (chapters 4-14) catalogs Israel's moral corruption and empty worship, declares that judgment is coming, and closes with the promise that God will heal their backsliding and love them freely once again.
hos.keyPoints: Using marriage as a picture, the book exposes Israel's unfaithfulness alongside God's unwavering love, and calls the people to forsake their idols and return to the LORD.

isa.background: Isaiah, the eighth-century-BC prophet to Judah, ministered through the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, warning that Judah's sin would bring judgment through Assyria and Babylon. The book falls into two major sections: chapters 1-39 largely concern judgment, condemning the rebellion of Judah and the surrounding nations, interspersed with promises of a coming messianic king (such as 7:14 and 9:6); chapters 40-66 turn to a message of comfort and restoration, announcing that God will redeem his people through a suffering servant (chapter 53) and promising a new heaven and a new earth.
isa.keyPoints: The core message is that God will judge sin, yet accomplishes redemption through his suffering messianic servant, granting restoration and everlasting hope.

jas.background: James is traditionally attributed to James the brother of the Lord Jesus, leader of the Jerusalem church, writing to Jewish believers scattered abroad who were undergoing trials and persecution. Written in the style of wisdom literature, the letter is direct and practical, urging believers to endure trials patiently and to live out a genuine faith. It insists that faith without works is dead, and addresses controlling the tongue, wisdom that comes from above, showing no favoritism, and the power of prayer, closing with an appeal to pray for one another and to bring back those who have wandered from the truth.
jas.keyPoints: The central theme is that genuine faith proves itself in action: true faith inevitably bears fruit in loving deeds and a holy life, and believers are urged to endure trials with patience, relying on the wisdom that comes from God.

jdg.background: Judges records the dark period between the death of Joshua and Samuel's anointing of Saul, when Israel was governed by judges; tradition attributes the book to Samuel. The opening section (chapters 1-2) describes how Canaan was left incompletely conquered and sets out the recurring cycle: the people sin, fall under oppression, cry out, and God raises up a judge to deliver them. The central section (chapters 3-16) recounts, in turn, the exploits of twelve judges, including Othniel, Deborah, Gideon, and Samson. The closing section (chapters 17-21) is an appendix describing the disorders of the age - Micah's idol, the outrage against the Levite's concubine - reflecting the moral collapse of a time when "every man did that which was right in his own eyes."
jdg.keyPoints: The central theme is the recurring cycle of forsaking God and falling under oppression, then repenting and being delivered; the chaos of an age with no king, when everyone did as he pleased, points to the need for a king after God's own heart.

jer.background: Jeremiah, the seventh-to-sixth-century-BC prophet to Judah known as "the weeping prophet," ministered from the reign of Josiah through Zedekiah and personally witnessed Jerusalem's fall to Babylon. The book repeatedly calls the people to repentance and warns of judgment if they refuse, while also recording Jeremiah's own persecution and anguished inner struggles. It also announces that God will one day establish a new covenant (chapter 31), writing his law on human hearts. The closing sections recount the fall of Judah and prophecies against the surrounding nations.
jer.keyPoints: The core message is that refusal to repent brings judgment, yet God faithfully promises a new covenant, writing his law on human hearts and forgiving iniquity.

job.background: Job, whose author is unknown, is traditionally thought to date from around the time of Moses or earlier, and stands as a masterpiece of Old Testament wisdom literature. Set in what appears to be the patriarchal era, it tells of Job, a godly non-Israelite who suffers immense affliction. The opening two chapters, in prose, describe Satan's accusation against Job before God, and the loss in quick succession of his children, his wealth, and his health. What follows (chapters 3-31) is a three-round poetic debate between Job and his three friends - Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar - wrestling with the relationship between suffering and God's justice. Elihu speaks in chapters 32-37, and in chapters 38-41 God himself answers Job out of the whirlwind, displaying his wisdom and power. In the closing chapter, Job humbles himself and repents, and God restores him twofold.
job.keyPoints: Suffering does not always come as a result of sin; in the midst of affliction we are called to trust God's sovereignty and wisdom, rather than demand a full explanation for it.

joe.background: Little is known of Joel, the author, or of when he wrote. Using a devastating locust plague and drought that struck the land of Judah (chapter 1) as a warning sign, he announces that a far greater 'day of the LORD' is coming, and calls the people to fast, repent, and rend their hearts rather than their garments (first half of chapter 2). God promises mercy - restoring the rains and pouring out his Spirit on all flesh (second half of chapter 2). The final chapter (3) declares that God will judge the nations and vindicate his people, and that Judah will be blessed forever.
joe.keyPoints: The locust plague foreshadows the day of the LORD and calls for genuine repentance; the promised outpouring of the Spirit finds its fulfillment at Pentecost.

joh.background: John is traditionally attributed to the apostle John, and its content differs markedly from the other three Gospels: it contains almost no parables, but instead gives detailed accounts of Jesus' conversations with individuals, seven miraculous "signs," and seven "I am" declarations, all displaying his divine glory. The Gospel states its purpose explicitly (20:31): that people may believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life through believing. Its structure divides broadly into the "Book of Signs" (chapters 1-12) and the teaching and events surrounding his suffering, death, and ascension (chapters 13-21).
joh.keyPoints: The central message is that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; through believing in his name, people receive eternal life - this is the very purpose for which the book was written.

jon.background: Jonah tells how God sent the prophet Jonah to proclaim a message of repentance to Nineveh, capital of Assyria, Israel's hated enemy. Jonah instead fled toward Tarshish; a storm arose at sea, he was thrown overboard, and a great fish swallowed him (chapter 1). From inside the fish he prayed in repentance and was delivered by God (chapter 2). He finally obeyed and went to Nineveh, and to his astonishment the whole city repented and was spared (chapter 3). Yet Jonah was displeased that God showed mercy, so God used a gourd plant to teach him that his love extends to all peoples (chapter 4).
jon.keyPoints: The book reveals that God's mercy extends to the Gentile nations as well, challenging narrow national pride and teaching believers to view the world with God's own compassion.

jos.background: Joshua records the history of Israel's entry into Canaan under Joshua's leadership after the death of Moses; tradition attributes the book to Joshua himself, with the account of his death likely added by a later hand. It falls into three parts: the first (chapters 1-12) tells of the crossing of the Jordan and the conquest campaigns, including the fall of Jericho and Ai; the second (chapters 13-21) records the division of the land among the tribes and the establishment of the Levitical cities and cities of refuge; the third (chapters 22-24) recounts Joshua's farewell exhortation, urging the people to renew the covenant and serve the LORD faithfully.
jos.keyPoints: The central theme is God's faithfulness in fulfilling his promise of the land; the book stresses that only by being strong and of good courage, and by carefully keeping the law, does one prosper, and it calls the people to serve the LORD alone.

jud.background: Jude is traditionally attributed to Jude, brother of the Lord Jesus and brother of James. He had intended to write about the salvation all believers share, but on learning that ungodly men had secretly slipped into the church, twisting grace into a license for immorality, he instead wrote urgently to call believers to contend earnestly for the faith. He cites examples of apostasy from the Old Testament as warnings, denounces the corrupt conduct of the false teachers, and urges believers to build themselves up, to pray in the Holy Spirit, and to keep themselves in the love of God - closing with the well-known doxology.
jud.keyPoints: The central theme is a warning against apostasy and false teachers infiltrating the church, urging believers to contend earnestly for the faith and to keep themselves in the love of God as they watch and wait for the Lord.

lam.background: Lamentations is traditionally attributed to the prophet Jeremiah, mourning the fall of Jerusalem and the destruction of the temple in 586 BC. The book consists of five laments (chapters 1-5); the first four are written as Hebrew acrostics, each line weighted with grief yet never wholly without hope. Chapter 3, at the book's center, turns from the depths of suffering to look upon God's faithfulness and mercy, becoming the turning point of the whole book. The closing chapter ends with a plea for God to restore his people, weaving together confession, sorrow, and persevering hope.
lam.keyPoints: Even amid the utter devastation of a fallen nation, the book holds fast to the conviction that the LORD's mercies are new every morning - teaching us to hold on to hope, confess our sin, and repent in the midst of suffering.

lev.background: Leviticus, traditionally attributed to Moses, records the laws God gave Moses at Mount Sinai, following the completion of the tabernacle in Exodus and before the people set out on their journey. The book falls into several sections: the sacrificial regulations (chapters 1-7); the ordination of the priests (chapters 8-10); the laws of clean and unclean (chapters 11-15); the Day of Atonement (chapter 16); and a comprehensive code for holy living (chapters 17-27), covering ethics, festivals, the sabbatical year, and the Year of Jubilee. Its central call is, "Ye shall be holy: for I the LORD your God am holy."
lev.keyPoints: The central theme is God's holiness and his provision for atonement: sin is covered through sacrifice, the whole nation is cleansed on the Day of Atonement, and the people are called to be set apart as holy and to draw near to God.

luk.background: Luke was written by the physician Luke, addressed to Theophilus, who set out to compile an orderly account of the life of Jesus after careful investigation; it is the companion volume to the Acts of the Apostles. The Gospel gives particular attention to the details of Jesus' birth and to the mercy and salvation he showed toward tax collectors, sinners, women, Gentiles, and the poor and oppressed, and it records Jesus at prayer and the work of the Holy Spirit at many points throughout. Its structure moves broadly through Jesus' ministry in Galilee (chapters 4-9), his teaching on the journey to Jerusalem (chapters 9-19), and his suffering and resurrection (chapters 19-24).
luk.keyPoints: The central message is that Jesus Christ came to seek and save the lost, showing mercy to the marginalized and the lowly; salvation has come to all people, without regard to rank or status.

mal.background: Malachi is the last book of the Old Testament. Little is known of Malachi, the author, and the book was written after the temple had been rebuilt following the return from exile, at a time when the people's faith had grown cold and merely formal. The book unfolds through a series of questions and answers in which God rebukes the priests for offering blind and lame animals as sacrifices and treating temple service with contempt, and rebukes the people for divorcing their wives in breach of covenant and withholding their tithes. It closes with the promise that the LORD's messenger will come to prepare the way, and that before the great and dreadful day, God will send Elijah to turn the hearts of the people, lest the land be struck with a curse.
mal.keyPoints: At the heart of the book is a rebuke of cold, formal religion and a call to sincere worship and covenant faithfulness; it also promises that a messenger will come to prepare the way for the great and dreadful day of the Lord.

mar.background: Mark is traditionally attributed to John Mark, recording the eyewitness testimony of the apostle Peter. It is the shortest and most fast-paced of the four Gospels, repeatedly using the word "immediately" to highlight the swift, powerful action of Jesus. The book presents Jesus above all as the suffering Servant: the first section (chapters 1-8) recounts his mighty works, the middle section (chapters 8-10) records three predictions of his death and resurrection, and the final section (chapters 11-16) narrates his suffering in Jerusalem, his crucifixion, and his resurrection - calling disciples to take up their cross and follow him.
mar.keyPoints: The central message is that Jesus Christ came as a servant, giving his life as a ransom for many; disciples are called to follow his example, taking up their cross and serving humbly to the end.

mat.background: Matthew is traditionally attributed to the apostle Matthew (Levi the tax collector), and it was written primarily for a Jewish readership. It repeatedly cites Old Testament prophecy to demonstrate that Jesus is the long-promised Messiah, the son of David, and the King of heaven. The book is structured around five major discourses woven together with narrative: the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5-7), the commissioning of the twelve disciples (chapter 10), the parables of the kingdom of heaven (chapter 13), teaching on church life (chapter 18), and the Olivet Discourse on the last things (chapters 24-25) - all framed by the birth, death, and resurrection of Jesus, and the Great Commission (chapter 28).
mat.keyPoints: At the heart of the book is Jesus as the Messiah-King who came to fulfill Old Testament prophecy; he calls disciples to be citizens of the kingdom of heaven, obeying his teaching, until it reaches all nations.

mic.background: Micah, the author, was from Moresheth in Judah and prophesied to both Judah and Israel during the same period as Isaiah. The book unfolds in three cycles that alternate between judgment and hope: chapters 1-2 rebuke the people's sin and predict judgment, yet promise that a remnant will be gathered; chapters 3-5 condemn the corruption of the rulers, priests, and prophets, and foretell that the Messiah will be born in Bethlehem and establish a kingdom of peace; chapters 6-7 close with God's case against his people, presenting the summons to 'do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God,' ending in praise of God's faithfulness and love.
mic.keyPoints: The book's heart is the call to 'do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God,' together with the prophecy that the Messiah would be born in Bethlehem.

nah.background: Little is known of Nahum, the author, apart from his hometown of Elkosh. He prophesied around the seventh century BC, as Nineveh, capital of Assyria, was about to fall - roughly a century after Jonah had been sent to call the city to repentance, and by this time Nineveh had returned to its old cruelty and arrogance. The book falls into three parts: the first chapter declares the LORD's character as one who is jealous and avenging, yet gracious to those who take refuge in him; the second chapter vividly depicts the fall of Nineveh; the final chapter recounts Nineveh's crimes - bloodshed, sorcery, and oppression of the nations - and declares that God's righteous judgment will surely come.
nah.keyPoints: At the heart of the book is God's righteous judgment: the proud and violent empire will certainly fall; God repays his enemies, yet strengthens and shows grace to those who take refuge in him.

neh.background: Nehemiah draws largely on Nehemiah's own memoirs. Serving as cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes, Nehemiah heard that Jerusalem's walls lay in ruins and asked leave to return and rebuild them. The first part (chapters 1-7) tells how he prayed, planned, and led the people in rebuilding the wall - completing it in just fifty-two days despite mockery and opposition from Sanballat and others. The middle section (chapters 8-10) recounts Ezra reading the law aloud, the people confessing their sin, entering into covenant, and keeping the Feast of Tabernacles. The final section (chapters 11-13) records the dedication of the wall, the resettling of the population, and the reforms Nehemiah carried out on a later return, addressing abuses of the Sabbath, intermarriage, and other lingering problems.
neh.keyPoints: Through prayer and dependence on God, and through steady, persevering labor, the wall-building mission was accomplished; renewal came to the people's lives through the law as well, bearing witness that faith and action must go hand in hand.

num.background: Numbers, traditionally attributed to Moses, records Israel's departure from Mount Sinai, their nearly forty years of wandering in the wilderness, and their arrival at the plains of Moab in preparation for entering Canaan; the book's name comes from the two censuses it records. It falls into three sections: the mustering and departure of the tribes from Sinai (chapters 1-10); the wilderness rebellion - the people's complaints, the spies' bad report, and God's judgment condemning the unbelieving generation to forty years of wandering (chapters 11-25); and the numbering of the new generation as they prepare to take possession of the land (chapters 26-36). Throughout, the book displays both God's judgment on a rebellious people and his guidance of those who trust him.
num.keyPoints: The central theme is God's judgment on rebellion alongside his faithfulness to his promise: though one generation perished in the wilderness for their unbelief, God still led the new generation into Canaan.

oba.background: Obadiah is the shortest book in the Old Testament, a single chapter, and nothing certain is known of its author. Its message is directed against Edom - the descendants of Esau, Jacob's brother - because the Edomites gloated over Jerusalem's disaster, stood aloof or joined in, and even plundered and killed the people of Judah. God declares that Edom will be utterly destroyed for its pride and violence. The book closes with the promise that the house of Jacob will be delivered and will recover its lost territory, and that the kingdom of the LORD will finally be established.
oba.keyPoints: The book declares that God will vindicate his oppressed people and judge pride and gloating over others' misfortune, revealing the kingdom of the LORD's sovereign rule.

phi.background: Philippians was written by Paul from prison to the church at Philippi, which he had founded and which had consistently and generously supported him; the letter thanks them for their gift and gives news of his circumstances. It is a letter overflowing with joy: Paul urges believers to be of one mind, following the example of Christ's willing humility, self-emptying, and obedience even to death (chapters 1-2); he warns against Judaizing legalists, counting all things as loss for the sake of knowing Christ and gaining the hope of resurrection (chapter 3); and in the final section he teaches believers to pray with joy and thanksgiving, testifying that he can do all things through him who gives him strength (chapter 4).
phi.keyPoints: The central message is rejoicing in Christ always: believers are called to follow Christ's humble, self-giving example, finding contentment, strength, and thankful prayer in him whatever their circumstances.

phm.background: Philemon is Paul's shortest and most personal letter, written from prison to Philemon, a believer in Colossae, pleading on behalf of his runaway slave Onesimus. Having fled his master, Onesimus came to faith in Christ while with Paul in prison; Paul now sends him back, appealing to Philemon to receive him no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother, and even offering to repay whatever Onesimus owes. The letter overflows with the spirit of forgiveness and acceptance found in Christ, showing how the gospel transforms human relationships.
phm.keyPoints: The central theme is forgiveness and acceptance in Christ: the gospel turns master and slave into brothers, and believers are urged to forgive graciously and welcome those who repent.

pro.background: Proverbs is a work of wisdom literature attributed mainly to King Solomon, though it also includes the sayings of the wise (22:17-24:34), the words of Agur (chapter 30), and the teaching of King Lemuel (chapter 31). The opening section (chapters 1-9) takes the form of a father instructing his son, contrasting wisdom and folly. The middle section (chapters 10-29) gathers terse, memorable sayings covering character, speech, diligence, relationships, and countless other facets of daily life. The book closes with the well-known portrait of the "virtuous woman." Its guiding theme is that "the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom."
pro.keyPoints: The core message is that the fear of the LORD is the foundation of wisdom; the book teaches how to live out God's wisdom in every area of daily life.

psa.background: Psalms is Israel's collected book of worship songs, 150 in all, composed by many different authors over several centuries. David is the foremost among them, alongside Asaph, the sons of Korah, Solomon, Moses, and others. Tradition divides the book into five sections (1-41; 42-72; 73-89; 90-106; 107-150), echoing the five books of Moses. Its content spans hymns of praise, songs of thanksgiving, laments, wisdom psalms, and royal or messianic psalms, giving voice to heartfelt worship, cries for help, and trust poured out before God.
psa.keyPoints: Psalms teaches wholehearted trust in the LORD through both praise and sorrow, points forward to the messianic king, and guides believers to pour out their hearts honestly before God.

rev.background: Revelation is traditionally attributed to the apostle John, written while he was exiled and persecuted on the isle of Patmos, where the Lord Jesus revealed to him a series of visions. It belongs to the genre of apocalyptic literature and is rich in symbolic imagery. The book falls into three sections: the first (chapters 1-3) records the Lord's words of praise and exhortation to the seven churches of Asia; the middle section (chapters 4-19) presents visions of worship in heaven and a succession of judgments falling upon the world; the final section (chapters 20-22) describes Christ's ultimate victory, the destruction of Satan, and the coming of the new heaven and new earth and the New Jerusalem, where God dwells with his people forever. Throughout, the book carries the message that Christ will surely triumph, and that believers are called to endure faithfully to the end.
rev.keyPoints: The central theme is that Christ will ultimately triumph and evil will be judged, as God makes all things new; believers are urged to endure patiently through tribulation, watching and waiting for the Lord's return.

rom.background: Romans is a letter written by the apostle Paul to the church in Rome, composed near the end of his third missionary journey, before he carried the collection to Jerusalem. It is the most systematic theological treatise among the New Testament epistles. The letter divides into two main parts: doctrine (chapters 1–11) and life (chapters 12–16). The doctrinal section first argues that all humanity — Jew and Gentile alike — stands guilty of sin, and that no one can be justified by keeping the law, but only by faith; it goes on to address sanctification, peace with God, the indwelling Holy Spirit, and God's election of and plan of salvation for Israel. The practical section then urges believers to offer themselves as living sacrifices, to love one another, to submit to governing authorities, and to bear with those weak in faith.
rom.keyPoints: The central truth is justification by faith: all have sinned, yet are freely justified through faith by the redemption that is in Christ Jesus; believers are called to live out a life of holiness in response.

rut.background: Ruth tells the story of one godly family during the days of the judges; tradition attributes the book to Samuel. Driven by famine, Elimelech moves with his wife Naomi to Moab, where their son marries a Moabite woman, Ruth; after her husband and sons die, Ruth resolves to stay with Naomi and return with her to Bethlehem (chapter 1). There Ruth gleans in the fields of Boaz and finds favor with him (chapter 2); Naomi instructs Ruth to ask Boaz to fulfill his duty as near kinsman (chapter 3); Boaz marries Ruth and fathers Obed, becoming the great-grandfather of David (chapter 4).
rut.keyPoints: Through Boaz, the kinsman-redeemer, the book displays God's compassion and faithfulness amid suffering, advances the line of David, and foreshadows the redemption found in Christ.

sos.background: The Song of Solomon, traditionally attributed to Solomon, is a collection of poems celebrating the love between a bridegroom and his bride, presented as a dialogue that traces their courtship, betrothal, and the intimacy of married life, all in beautiful and tastefully restrained language. The book has no clear chapter divisions, and its movement follows the rise and fall of emotion rather than a linear plot. Traditional interpretation reads it as a celebration of the pure and beautiful love and intimacy of marriage as a gift from God; others have read it as an allegory foreshadowing the love between Christ and the church.
sos.keyPoints: It celebrates faithful, exclusive love within marriage as a good gift from God, and is also read as an allegory of Christ's self-giving love for the church.

tit.background: Titus is one of Paul's pastoral letters, written to instruct Titus in organizing the church on the island of Crete and appointing elders. The first chapter sets out the qualifications elders must meet and warns against the corrupt teaching of false teachers on the island; the second chapter describes the godly conduct expected of believers of every age and station, grounding it in Christ's self-giving redemption; the closing chapter urges believers to submit to rulers and to do good to all, stressing that salvation rests on God's mercy rather than human works - and precisely for that reason believers should be all the more devoted to doing good.
tit.keyPoints: The central theme is that sound doctrine must bear fruit in good works: saved through God's mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit, believers are called to be devoted to doing good.

zec.background: Zechariah, the author, was both priest and prophet, a contemporary of Haggai who likewise urged the people, after their return from exile, to rebuild the temple. The book falls into two main parts: the first section (chapters 1-8) records eight night visions calling the people to turn back to God, promising the restoration of Jerusalem, the cleansing of Joshua the high priest, and the rise of the Messiah as 'the Branch'; the second section (chapters 9-14) consists of two oracles foretelling that the Messiah would enter the city humbly, riding on a donkey, be pierced by his own companions, and that the shepherd would be struck and the sheep scattered - concluding with the declaration that after the nations make war, the LORD will finally triumph on the day of the LORD, and all the world will worship the true God.
zec.keyPoints: At the heart of the book is the promise of the Messiah: the humble king enters the city on a donkey and lays down his life for the sheep; in the end the LORD will triumph and reign, and all the world will worship him.

zep.background: Zephaniah, the author, appears from his genealogy to have been a descendant of King Hezekiah, and he prophesied during the reign of King Josiah of Judah, in the midst of Josiah's religious reforms. The book centers on 'the day of the LORD': the first chapter announces that God will judge Judah for idolatry and for adopting foreign customs; the second chapter announces judgment on the surrounding nations - Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Cush, and Assyria; the final chapter first rebukes the corrupt officials and priests of Jerusalem, then promises that after judgment a purified remnant will be saved, and that the LORD will rejoice over Zion and comfort his people with his love.
zep.keyPoints: At the heart of the book is the day of the LORD: judgment comes upon Judah and the nations, yet the chosen remnant will be purified and delivered, and God will rejoice over them in love.
